interactions.summary: A student argues that splitting the atom is unlike impossible alchemy because it is actually within the fabric of the universe, while Jiang keeps the focus on entering dangerous foundational territory.

Jiang answers by treating money as a successful human workaround for turning paper into gold and by insisting that where there is will and imagination, the sinful drive to distort order can still find an outlet.

claims.claim: Jiang says nuclear energy counts as alchemy because it enters the most fundamental fabric of nature without knowing the consequences of the act.
Jiang uses money as an analogue for successful alchemy by saying human beings already turn paper into gold-like purchasing power through symbolic intermediaries.
Jiang argues that Dante's real concern is not literal metallurgical success but malicious will joined to imagination, because where there is a will there can be a way around formal impossibility.
A student reinforces Jiang's line by linking alchemy to Tower-of-Babel ambition: the will to replace God and distort natural order repeats whenever humans keep pressing impossible projects.

signature_moments.moment: Paper money becomes Jiang's proof that people really can perform a social version of turning lead into gold.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is his most surprising move for collapsing symbolic finance into Dante's fraud category.

signature_moments.moment: The danger lies in never underestimating human imagination once it sets malicious intent on a target.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we can never ever underestimate the human imagination
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It converts the alchemy discussion from technical feasibility to anthropological power.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's claim that symbolic systems can convert worthless matter into effective wealth, making alchemy socially real even if metallurgy fails.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang cites fringe claims about nuclear bombs opening portals to demons or aliens as an illustration of how people imagine nuclear technology; this should not be treated as his settled empirical claim.
